title: CPU-side bottlenecks investigation - tokenization, request parsing, thread pools, Python overhead
content:
Summary:

This note captures recent profiling and benchmark work investigating CPU-side bottlenecks in the serving runtime. Focus areas: tokenization, request parsing/JSON overhead, thread-pool design (GIL and context switching), and general Python-level overheads that surface during high QPS workloads. Goal is to prioritize mitigations that give the best latency/cost wins with minimal infra changes.

Environment & workload details:
- runtime: serving-runtime v1.9.3 (local dev build with debug symbols stripped)
- model: distil-*-like text-generation model (tokenization + model I/O path exercised; model inference runs on GPU where applicable, but this investigation isolates CPU-side work)
- hardware: c8i.8xlarge-equivalent (32 vCPU logical cores), 64GB RAM; tests also run on 8-core dev machines
- concurrency: 100 concurrent connections simulated via locust/wrk; payload sizes: short prompts (avg 40 tokens), medium (200 tokens), long (1k tokens)
- request format: JSON POST to /v1/generate with prompt, options. Baseline uses JSON and standard Python json.loads/ dumps (ujson not used).
- tokenizers: HuggingFace Python tokenizer wrapper (tokenizers v0.13 using Rust bindings) in baseline, but tokenizer is re-instantiated per request in the current server code path (identified as suspicious).

Profiling methodology:
- py-spy top (sampling) to get CPU-per-function hotspots under load
- py-spy record --flamegraph to produce flamegraphs for critical experiments
- perf + FlameGraph on native code for native-library hotspots
- tracemalloc for allocation hotspots in Python
- microbenchmarks for isolated components (tokenization.py:bench.py, json-parse bench, threadpool task latency)
- test harness: deterministic seed; runs repeated 10x to smooth noise

Key findings (high level):
1) Tokenization is often the single-largest CPU consumer for short/medium prompts when model forward is on GPU. Observed 25-45% of total CPU time allocated to tokenization functions in py-spy flamegraphs for medium prompts.
2) Request parsing + JSON serialization contributes ~10-18% of CPU time; pathological cases (huge option blobs) spike this to 30% for large requests.
3) Thread pools + GIL interactions: thread worker wakeups + small tasks incur non-trivial context switching. In our threadpool-based request model, we see elevated sys/sched time (~12%) and frequent short-lived Python threads waiting on GIL, increasing tail latency under high QPS.
4) Python allocation churn (short-lived dicts/objects) shows up in tracemalloc and correlates with GC pauses adding ~5-12ms to tail latency in 95th/99th latency.
5) Repeated instantiation of tokenizer objects per-request (observed in current code path) is a major anti-pattern — single tokenizer instantiation reused across requests reduces tokenization CPU by ~30% in microbenchmarks.

Representative numbers (medium prompt, 200 tokens, 100 concurrent clients):
- baseline median CPU time per request (non-GPU parts): ~18.6 ms
  - tokenization: 7.1 ms (38%)
  - request parsing (json.loads + validation): 3.0 ms (16%)
  - request routing + auth checks: 2.3 ms (12%)
  - thread scheduling/overhead: 2.1 ms (11%)
  - other Python logic (metrics, logging): 1.8 ms (10%)
  - allocation/GC tail: ~2.3 ms occasional spikes
- after quick wins (reuse tokenizer, use ujson, pre-compiled routing regex, pool warmup): median non-GPU CPU time per request drops to ~10.2 ms
  - tokenization: 4.3 ms
  - request parsing: 1.4 ms
  - scheduling/overhead: 1.5 ms

Detailed observations & evidence:
- Tokenizer instantiation
  - baseline code constructs Tokenizer(...) per HTTP request inside request handler. py-spy flamegraphs clearly show constructor overhead and associated allocations. Microbenchmark: instantiating tokenizer 1000x took ~420 ms vs reusable tokenizer encode call 1000x ~110 ms on same machine.
  - Reuse approach: create a pool of tokenizer instances (one per worker process or a shared async-safe instance if using tokenizer Rust bindings) and reuse per-request. This lowers allocations and avoids repeated Rust->Python FFI setup.

- JSON parsing & schema validation
  - json.loads is visible in hotspots. Replacing with ujson or orjson yields 1.8–2.2x speedups in parse/serialize.
  - In addition, deep validation (per-field checks) implemented in Python is a source of CPU cost. Consider lightweight validation (schema checks in C: pydantic v2 or fastjsonschema) or move heavy validation to a separate path (async pre-validation).

- Thread pool design and GIL behaviour
  - Current model: thread-per-request worker pool implemented with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor handling small CPU-bound pre/post processing tasks while model inference is handed to GPU threads. Under high concurrency, we see GIL contention and many threads in the 'waiting for GIL' state.
  - Switching to process-based workers (multiprocessing) isolates GIL but increases memory footprint. For our workload, moving heavy CPU tasks (tokenization + parsing) into a small number of worker processes reduced tail latency by ~18% at 100 QPS with acceptable memory cost.
  - Another option: keep thread pool but offload CPU-heavy parts into native extensions (Rust/C++) or use the tokenizers Rust binding which releases the GIL during encode. Verify that tokenizers.encode() actually releases GIL in our binding; if not, wrap in a C extension or call out to a worker process.

- Python allocation churn and logging
  - Tracemalloc shows many short-lived dicts from request context building and structured logging. Reducing structured logging frequency and reusing per-thread buffers reduced allocation churn in experiments.
  - Use of logging in hot path should be guarded; use sampling for debug logs in production.

Mitigations & recommended next steps (priority ordered):
1) Immediate low-effort wins (<=2 days dev):
   - Reuse tokenizer instance(s) instead of per-request instantiation. Implement as: one tokenizer per worker process (if using Gunicorn/uvicorn) or a small LRU pool.
   - Replace json.loads/json.dumps with orjson/ujson in hot paths and benchmark for compatibility.
   - Switch to or add pydantic v2 (or fastjsonschema) for faster validation or push validation outside hot path.
2) Medium effort (1–3 weeks):
   - Move tokenization into native (Rust) path that releases GIL (if current binding holds GIL). Confirm with C-level profiling.
   - Batch tokenization for requests that arrive from the same connection or short window (micro-batching) to amortize per-call overhead.
   - Evaluate process-based worker model for CPU-heavy pre/post processing (tradeoff: memory vs. lower GIL contention).
3) Longer-term / engineering-heavy (3–8 weeks):
   - Rework request pipeline to use a binary protocol (msgpack/gRPC) for internal agent-to-agent calls to avoid JSON overhead.
   - Implement zero-copy parsing where possible, and reuse buffers (memory pools, jemalloc tuning).
   - Consider a native C++/Rust front-end for parsing/ tokenization that streams tokens into the existing runtime.

Quantified impact goals (targets to validate):
- Reduce non-GPU CPU per-request baseline by 40–60% for short/medium prompts via tokenizer reuse + JSON improvement.
- Reduce 95th/99th tail latency by 20–35% at 2x concurrent load through process worker isolation or native tokenization releasing GIL.

Experiments to run next (owners & tickets):
- EXP-401: Implement tokenizer pooling & benchmark (owner: Daniel Kim) — Jira: JIRA-RT-2242
- EXP-402: Replace JSON parser with orjson and run end-to-end QPS/latency tests (owner: Priya Natarajan) — Jira: JIRA-RT-2243
- EXP-403: Small process pool prototype for pre/post CPU tasks (owner: Marco Alvarez) — Jira: JIRA-RT-2244
- EXP-404: Instrument tokenizer Rust binding to confirm GIL release (owner: Asha Rao) — Jira: JIRA-RT-2245

Open questions / risks:
- Compatibility of orjson/orjson default behavior with our schema (e.g., datetime handling) — need regression tests.
- Memory cost of moving to process-based workers in Dedicated deployments with constrained nodes — run capacity planning.
- Some customers will require private deployments with strict libc/allocator constraints; validate jemalloc/ld_preload interactions.
- Potential subtle differences in tokenization if using different tokenizer versions or moving to a native tokenizer service; must pin tokenizer models and include tokenization unit tests.

Notes & implementation hints:
- For quick checks use: py-spy top --pid <pid> and py-spy record --output=flame.svg --pid <pid> while running load.
- To measure JSON: python -m timeit -s "import json; s='{"prompt":"hi"}'" "json.loads(s)" and compare vs orjson.loads.
- Tokenizer microbenchmark: create a script that measures tokenizer.encode(prompt) 10k times to spot per-call overhead.
- Use pmap/numactl to pin worker processes to cores in CD environments to reduce cross-socket penalties.

Appendix: quick microbenchmark results (dev machine, 8-core):
- tokenizer instantiate + encode (1000 reps): 420 ms
- tokenizer encode only (reuse instance, 1000 reps): 110 ms
- json.loads (100k reps): 420 ms
- orjson.loads (100k reps): 180 ms
- small-threadpool task latency median (1000 tasks): 1.9 ms (threadpool), 1.5 ms (process pool)

Conclusion:
CPU-side work is a first-class signal even for GPU-backed inference: tokenization + request parsing + Python overhead are responsible for a significant portion of non-GPU latency and cost. We can obtain large wins with modest changes (tokenizer reuse + faster JSON library + small pipeline optimizations). Medium-term native/Rust offload and process-isolation can further stabilize tail latency.
